course.title: Introduction to Sociology
course.description: A first tour of how societies work — the sociological perspective, research methods, culture, socialization, groups, deviance, and stratification. Structure adapted from OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e (CC BY 4.0).

questions.explanation: Sociology studies patterns in groups and society — see 'The sociological perspective'.

lessons.title: The sociological perspective and its theories
lessons.grammar_note: Macro = large structures; micro = face-to-face interaction.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define the sociological perspective and contrast the three major theoretical paradigms. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, whose idea connects *personal troubles* to *public issues*?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sociology is the *scientific* study of society and social behavior. Its core move is the *sociological imagination* (C. Wright Mills): seeing a private experience — losing a job, getting married — as shaped by larger social forces. Three paradigms organize the field. *Structural functionalism* (Durkheim) treats society as interdependent parts that each contribute to stability. *Conflict theory* (Marx) treats society as a struggle over scarce resources and power. *Symbolic interactionism* (Mead, Blumer) works at the micro level, studying the meanings people build through everyday interaction.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take unemployment. A functionalist asks how joblessness affects the stability of the whole system. A conflict theorist asks *who benefits* from having a pool of unemployed workers competing for wages. An interactionist asks how being labeled 'unemployed' reshapes a person's identity and daily interactions. Same fact, three lenses.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each question to a paradigm: (1) 'How does religion hold a community together?' (2) 'How do the wealthy use schooling to keep their advantage?' (3) 'What does a wedding ring *mean* to the people wearing it?' (4) 'What functions do sports serve for society?' Answers: 1-functionalism, 2-conflict, 3-symbolic interactionism, 4-functionalism.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the paradigms as right-vs-wrong instead of different lenses on the same reality. Mistake: confusing micro and macro (interactionism is micro; the other two are macro). Exit: (a) Which paradigm is micro-level? (b) Which paradigm emphasizes competition over power? Answers: symbolic interactionism; conflict theory.

lessons.title: How sociologists do research
lessons.grammar_note: Correlation is not causation — keep that phrase handy all course.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the main sociological research methods and explain why design and ethics matter. Warm-up: which method has you *join* a group rather than survey it from outside?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sociologists test ideas with evidence, not hunches. To do that they *operationalize* a concept — turn a fuzzy idea like 'religiosity' into something countable, such as services attended per month. The main methods are the *survey* (standardized questions to a sample), the *interview* (open, in-depth talk), *field research* / participant observation and *ethnography* (studying people in their natural setting), the *experiment* (manipulate one variable, control the rest), and *secondary data analysis* (reusing existing records). Good research relies on a representative *sample*, plus *reliability* (consistent results) and *validity* (measuring what you claim). Ethics require *informed consent* and protection from harm.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Claim: 'volunteering makes people happier.' Volunteers report more happiness, so the two *correlate* — but maybe happy people simply volunteer more, or a hidden factor (free time, income) drives both. Only a careful design can separate cause from a *confounding* variable. This is why correlation ≠ causation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each: (1) mailing 1,000 residents a questionnaire, (2) living in a fishing village for a year to record daily life, (3) analyzing decades of existing census records, (4) randomly assigning volunteers to two study-help programs and comparing grades. Answers: 1-survey, 2-ethnography/field research, 3-secondary analysis, 4-experiment.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a correlation proves cause. Mistake: generalizing from an unrepresentative sample. Exit: (a) Which method best supports a causal claim? (b) 'Consistent results on repeat' names which quality — reliability or validity? Answers: the experiment; reliability.

lessons.title: Culture: the shared design for living
lessons.grammar_note: Material culture = objects; nonmaterial culture = ideas and rules.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define culture and distinguish its parts, and tell ethnocentrism from cultural relativism. Warm-up: is a wedding ring *material* or *nonmaterial* culture?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Culture* is the shared beliefs, values, norms, symbols, and objects of a group. *Material culture* is the physical stuff (tools, buildings, clothing); *nonmaterial culture* is the ideas — *values* (broad ideals), *norms* (rules for behavior), and *symbols* including *language*. Norms range from *folkways* (everyday etiquette) to *mores* (strong moral rules) to *taboos* (near-universal prohibitions). Viewing another culture as inferior by your own standards is *ethnocentrism*; understanding it on its own terms is *cultural relativism*. A *subculture* differs from the mainstream; a *counterculture* actively opposes it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Eating with the hands is normal in many cultures and rude in others. An ethnocentric visitor calls it 'bad manners'; a culturally relative visitor asks what the practice means locally and follows the host's *folkways*. Same act, opposite judgments.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each: (1) a national flag, (2) the value 'honor your elders', (3) removing shoes before entering a home, (4) refusing to ever harm a sacred animal. Answers: 1-symbol (nonmaterial), 2-value, 3-folkway, 4-taboo/more.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing values (broad ideals) with norms (specific rules). Mistake: treating cultural relativism as 'anything goes' rather than as a tool for understanding. Exit: (a) Which norm carries the strongest moral weight — folkway or more? (b) Judging others by your own culture's standards is called…? Answers: more; ethnocentrism.

questions.prompt: Seeing a personal problem as shaped by larger social forces uses the…
questions.explanation: Mills's sociological imagination.

questions.prompt: Which paradigm centers on competition over scarce resources and power?
questions.explanation: Conflict theory, rooted in Marx.

questions.prompt: Living inside a community for a year to record its daily life is…
questions.explanation: Field research in the natural setting.

questions.prompt: Turning a fuzzy concept into something measurable is called…
questions.explanation: Operationalization makes a variable countable.

questions.prompt: A taboo differs from a folkway because it…
questions.explanation: Taboos are the strongest norms.

questions.prompt: Judging another culture as inferior by your own standards is…
questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism; relativism is its opposite.

lessons.title: Socialization: becoming a social self
lessons.grammar_note: Nature and nurture both shape the self — it isn't either/or.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how socialization builds the self and name its main agents. Warm-up: which single group first teaches a child the culture's basics?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Socialization* is the lifelong process of learning a society's culture and forming a *self*. It runs through *agents*: the *family* (the earliest and strongest), *schools*, *peer groups*, and the *media*. Two classic theories explain the self. Cooley's *looking-glass self* says we build our self-image from how we imagine others see us. Mead argued the self has an *I* (spontaneous actor) and a *me* (the internalized expectations of others), and that children develop through the imitation, play, and game stages until they grasp the *generalized other* — society's overall viewpoint. Both *nature* (biology) and *nurture* (environment) matter.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A child playing 'teacher' takes the role of another person (Mead's play stage). Later, in a team game, the child must track *everyone's* role at once — the game stage — which is practice for holding the generalized other in mind as an adult.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Identify the agent or concept: (1) parents teaching table manners, (2) feeling embarrassed because you imagine classmates judging you, (3) learning teamwork rules in a soccer match, (4) absorbing beauty standards from advertising. Answers: 1-family, 2-looking-glass self, 3-game stage / generalized other, 4-media.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking socialization ends in childhood (it is lifelong — new jobs and roles keep resocializing us). Mistake: treating the self as purely inborn. Exit: (a) Whose concept is the looking-glass self? (b) What does Mead call society's overall viewpoint? Answers: Cooley; the generalized other.

lessons.title: Groups, organizations, and bureaucracy
lessons.grammar_note: Primary groups = intimate bonds; secondary groups = task-focused ties.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish types of social groups and describe Weber's ideal bureaucracy. Warm-up: is your family a *primary* or a *secondary* group?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *primary group* is small, intimate, and enduring (family, close friends); a *secondary group* is larger and organized around a task (a class, a committee). We define ourselves partly through *in-groups* (we belong) and *out-groups* (we don't), and we judge ourselves against *reference groups*. Group size matters: Simmel showed a *dyad* (two) is fragile while a *triad* (three) is more stable. Large *formal organizations* often run as *bureaucracies*. Weber's *ideal type* of bureaucracy has a clear *hierarchy*, explicit *rules*, *impersonality* (treat cases by the rulebook, not by favoritism), a *division of labor*, and advancement by *merit*. Ritzer's 'McDonaldization' extends these efficiency principles across modern life.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Why does a two-person startup collapse when one founder leaves, while a three-person team survives? In a dyad each person is essential; in a triad the group persists even if one leaves — Simmel's point about group size and stability.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each: (1) a lifelong friendship, (2) a temporary project committee, (3) a sports team you admire and measure yourself against, (4) a rival school's fans. Answers: 1-primary group, 2-secondary group, 3-reference group, 4-out-group.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming 'bureaucracy' just means red tape — for Weber it is a rational model with real strengths. Mistake: mixing up in-group (belonging) with reference group (comparison). Exit: (a) Which is more stable, a dyad or a triad? (b) Name one feature of Weber's ideal bureaucracy. Answers: the triad; hierarchy / explicit rules / impersonality / division of labor / merit-based advancement.

items.translation: the ability to see personal experiences as shaped by larger social forces
items.example: The sociological imagination links one person's job loss to economic change.

items.translation: a shared rule or expectation about how members of a society should behave
items.example: Waiting your turn in line is an everyday norm.

items.translation: the lifelong process of learning a society's culture and forming a social self
items.example: Family is the first agent of socialization.

items.translation: behavior that violates a society's norms and draws a social reaction
items.example: What counts as deviance varies from culture to culture.

items.translation: the formal and informal mechanisms a society uses to enforce its norms
items.example: Laws and disapproving looks are both forms of social control.

items.translation: a society's ranking of people into layers of unequal wealth, power, and prestige
items.example: Social stratification shapes who has access to good schools.

questions.prompt: The earliest and usually strongest agent of socialization is the…
questions.explanation: Family teaches culture first.

questions.prompt: Cooley's 'looking-glass self' says our self-image comes from…
options: how we imagine others see us
questions.explanation: We mirror others' imagined views.

questions.prompt: A small, intimate, lasting group such as a family is a…
questions.explanation: Primary groups feature close, enduring bonds.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a feature of Weber's ideal bureaucracy?
questions.explanation: Bureaucracy is impersonal and merit-based, not favoritism-based.

questions.prompt: Behavior that violates social norms and draws a reaction is…
questions.explanation: Deviance is defined by norm violation and reaction.

questions.prompt: Ranking people into layers of unequal wealth and power is…
questions.explanation: Social stratification structures inequality.

lessons.title: Applied project: read a social setting like a sociologist

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one ordinary public setting you can observe (a cafe, a bus stop, a checkout line, a waiting room). Plan a small field observation of the *norms* and *interactions* there, then analyze it through one of the three paradigms. You will not need to run a full study — you'll design it rigorously and interpret what you'd expect to find.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Write one clear question about behavior in your setting (e.g. 'How do strangers signal they want to be left alone?'). 2) Define exactly what you would observe and how you'd record it, and name one ethical concern (consent, privacy). 3) Identify at least two norms at work, and whether any are folkways or mores. 4) Analyze the setting through one paradigm — functionalist, conflict, or symbolic interactionist — and say what that lens highlights.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Question is specific and answerable by observation. ✔ Your method is operationally defined so someone else could replicate it, and you flagged an ethics issue. ✔ You named real norms and classified at least one correctly. ✔ Your paradigm analysis fits the lens you chose (micro meanings for interactionism; power for conflict; stability/function for functionalism). If all four hold, you've analyzed a setting like a sociologist.
